title: Sell Mineral Rights in Doddridge County, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Doddridge County, WV | West Union
metaDescription: Doddridge County, WV sits at the heart of the Marcellus core with dense Antero development. We buy mineral rights and heir shares here, title-checked first.
heroLead: Doddridge County is about as close to the epicenter of the Marcellus core as any county in West Virginia gets, and its mineral ownership record reflects the intensity of that development as much as its rural, small-town character.
intro: West Union, the county seat, has processed an outsized volume of leases, pooling orders, and title work relative to its size over the last fifteen years, largely driven by Antero Resources' extensive development across the county. For mineral owners here, that means an unusually high chance of already sitting inside an active, multi-well unit, but it also means an unusually tangled title picture, because so much of this county's land was farmland held by families for generations before the drilling arrived.

We buy oil and gas mineral and royalty interests throughout Doddridge County directly, working from the actual recorded lease, unit order, and probate history for your specific tract rather than a general county-wide estimate.

sections.heading: The densest development in the state
paragraphs: Doddridge County has seen some of the most concentrated horizontal well pad development anywhere in West Virginia, with large multi-well pads drilled from centralized locations reaching out under many separate family tracts. A single Doddridge County mineral owner's decimal interest is frequently tied to a unit with several producing wells rather than one, which changes both the payment pattern and the way we evaluate the interest.

That density also means pooling orders here have been amended and re-amended over the years as additional wells were added to existing units. Confirming your current decimal interest requires checking the most recent order, not the one your family may remember from when the unit first formed.

sections.heading: Farmland that predates the boom
paragraphs: Before Antero and other operators arrived, Doddridge County was overwhelmingly rural and agricultural, small family farms scattered across rolling hill country. Those farms were typically owned outright for generations, which means when leasing arrived in force, a lot of ownership had already fragmented informally through inheritance, well before any lease was ever signed.

The result is a county with an unusually high concentration of undivided fractional interests: tracts where six, eight, or a dozen or more descendants of the same original farm family each hold a small percentage, often without a clean paper trail connecting them all.

sections.heading: Extreme heirship fragmentation
paragraphs: Doddridge County is a useful illustration of a pattern that shows up across rural Appalachia but is especially pronounced here: a mineral estate that was never formally divided on paper, passed by intestate succession through two or three generations, so that a fraction like one thirty-second or one sixty-fourth interest is entirely normal on an active, producing unit.

We buy individual heir shares at whatever fraction they actually represent, without requiring the rest of the family to agree or participate, and we do the work of establishing the chain of title, tracing wills where they exist and intestate succession where they don't, as part of the purchase rather than asking the seller to sort it out first.

It's not unusual to find that one branch of a family kept careful records while another lost track entirely, which means two cousins holding the same size interest can arrive at a sale with very different amounts of documentation. We work with whichever situation you're in.

sections.heading: Flat-rate leases predating the boom
paragraphs: Not every Doddridge County lease dates to the Marcellus era. Some tracts still carry older, shallow-well leases from decades before Antero's arrival, occasionally flat-rate leases that were never converted to West Virginia's statutory minimum one-eighth royalty. Where an old lease and a new Marcellus-era lease or unit order both touch the same tract, we read each on its own terms rather than assuming the newer lease supersedes the older one automatically.

faqs.question: How many wells are typically in a Doddridge County unit?
faqs.answer: It varies, but multi-well pads with three, four, or more producing wells sharing a single unit are common given the density of development here.

faqs.question: My family's interest is a very small fraction, like one sixty-fourth. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Fractional interests this small are typical in Doddridge County given generations of undivided inheritance, and we buy them once the exact percentage is confirmed.

faqs.question: How do you confirm my decimal interest if the unit has been amended multiple times?
faqs.answer: We pull the most recent pooling order on file, which reflects any amendments, rather than relying on the original order your family may be familiar with.

faqs.question: Do I need to probate my parents' estate before selling their Doddridge County interest?
faqs.answer: Not always. We can often work directly with heirship established through intestate succession, though a probated estate can simplify and speed up closing.

faqs.question: Can two leases, one old and one new, both cover the same Doddridge County tract?
faqs.answer: Yes, that's common where legacy shallow-well leases predate the Marcellus development. We review both instruments separately since they can carry different terms.

faqs.question: What paperwork speeds up an offer on a Doddridge County interest?
faqs.answer: A copy of any lease, division order, or probate document you have helps, but we can typically locate the recorded chain of title and current pooling order ourselves through the county Clerk's office in West Union.
